(CNN) -- Christine Beatty, chief of staff for former Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, pleaded guilty Monday to charges stemming from their text-messaging sex scandal case and will serve four months in jail, according to the Wayne County prosecutor's office. Under a plea deal, Christine Beatty, shown in August at an arraignment in Detroit, will serve five years probation. Beatty pleaded guilty to two counts of obstruction of justice, according to Maria Miller, the prosecutor's spokeswoman. Charges of perjury and misconduct against Beatty will be dropped as part of the plea arrangement, she said. Beatty agreed to a plea arrangement under which she will serve five years probation -- the first 120 days to be served in jail -- and pay a $100,000 fine, "based on [Beatty's] ability to pay," Miller said. Beatty will begin serving her jail sentence on January 5, when she will be formally sentenced, Miller said. Kym L. Worthy, prosecuting attorney for Wayne County, released a statement saying she is "very pleased that this defendant admitted her guilt." "We live in an age where greed and protecting one's secrets is glorified and accepted," Worthy said. "Now the city of Detroit, the region and the state of Michigan can truly begin to move forward when this ugly chapter in Detroit's history is put to rest." In September, Kilpatrick resigned as mayor and pleaded guilty to two felony obstruction of justice charges stemming from his efforts to cover up his relationship with Beatty. Like Beatty, Kilpatrick was sentenced to five years probation with the first four months to be served in jail. He is serving that sentence in the Wayne County jail. At the time of his sentencing in October, the judge in the case called Kilpatrick "arrogant and defiant," particularly for a televised speech that aired hours after Kilpatrick entered his pleas. "That night, the community expected to hear a message of humility, remorse and apology," Wayne County Circuit Judge David Groner said at Kilpatrick's sentencing. "Instead, we heard an arrogant and defiant man who accused the governor, among others, for his downfall." In addition to his jail and probation sentence, Kilpatrick must also pay the city of Detroit $1 million in restitution, and forfeit any future pension. Initially, Kilpatrick was accused of blocking a criminal investigation into his office and firing a police deputy to cover up an affair with Beatty, then his chief of staff. When that deputy, Gary Brown, filed a whistle-blower suit, Kilpatrick and Beatty denied under oath that an affair had taken place between them. Text messages that contradicted Kilpatrick's and Beatty's denials of an affair were made public in January by the Detroit Free Press, and county prosecutor Worthy charged Kilpatrick and Beatty with multiple counts of perjury, obstruction of justice and misconduct in office. The most serious charges would have carried a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison upon conviction. Beatty resigned her post after the text messages were made public. Kilpatrick initially refused to resign after the scandal broke, and Michigan Gov. Jennifer Granholm called a hearing on whether she should remove him from office at the request of the Detroit City Council. Granholm adjourned those hearings after Kilpatrick pleaded guilty and resigned in September.

**DETROIT (CNN)** — Christine Beatty, the former chief of staff and top aide to disgraced ex-Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, pleaded guilty Monday to two felony counts of obstruction of justice, agreeing to serve a 120-day jail sentence for lying under oath about her romantic relationship with her boss.

Beatty, 38, admitted in a Wayne County Circuit Court that she lied during a 2007 whistleblowers' trial when she denied having an affair with Kilpatrick and swore she was unaware of plans to fire a police official who was investigating the mayor’s security detail. 

"I lied under oath," a somber Beatty told the court, her voice barely above a whisper as she formally entered her plea. 

Under the terms of the plea agreement with Wayne County prosecutors, Beatty will serve 120 days in county jail, followed by five years of probation. She has also been ordered to pay $100,000 in restitution to the city of Detroit. 

The guilty plea marks the latest downfall in a political soap opera that has gripped Michigan’s largest city for nearly a year, shattering the promising career of Kilpatrick—once dubbed the "hip-hop mayor"—and tearing apart the city's leadership.

"Today is a step forward for justice in Wayne County," Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy said in a statement following the hearing. "This case was never about private lives. It was about public corruption, perjury, and the cover-up of illegal actions at the highest levels of city government."

The scandal erupted in January 2008 after *The Detroit Free Press* published excerpts from thousands of text messages sent from Beatty’s city-issued pager in 2002 and 2003. The messages contradicted testimony given by both Beatty and Kilpatrick during a civil trial brought by former Detroit police officers who claimed they were wrongfully demoted or fired for investigating corruption. 

While both Beatty and Kilpatrick testified under oath that they were merely close friends and professional colleagues, the text messages revealed a deeply intimate, romantic relationship. More critically, the text exchanges showed the pair discussing the dismissal of Deputy Police Chief Gary Brown, directly contradicting their sworn testimony.

The city subsequently paid a $9.7 million settlement to the police officers to keep the sexually explicit and politically damaging text messages secret. However, the release of the texts sparked a grand jury investigation led by Worthy, culminating in criminal charges against both officials.

Beatty’s guilty plea comes just months after Kilpatrick himself reached a similar deal. In September, Kilpatrick pleaded guilty to two counts of obstructing justice, resigned from office, and served 120 days in jail. He was also ordered to pay $1 million in restitution to the city and forfeit his law license.

Legal experts say Beatty’s plea effectively closes the chapter on the perjury phase of the scandal, though federal authorities are still reportedly investigating broader corruption allegations surrounding Kilpatrick's administration.

Beatty, who resigned as chief of staff in January shortly after the text messages were exposed, had previously faced up to 15 years in prison if convicted on all original charges, which included perjury and misconduct in office.

Judge Timothy Kenny set Beatty’s formal sentencing date for January 5, at which time she is expected to begin serving her jail term.

**DETROIT SPECIAL REPORT: The Legal Reckoning of Kwame Kilpatrick and Christine Beatty in the Text-Message Scandal**

**DETROIT —** What began as a civil lawsuit over internal police department politics culminated in one of the most explosive political scandals in American municipal history. The Detroit text-message scandal brought a dramatic end to the career of Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick—once dubbed the nation’s first "hip-hop mayor"—and his top aide, Chief of Staff Christine Beatty. 

The scandal exposed a web of perjury, official misconduct, and an extra-marital affair, resulting in felony convictions, jail time, million-dollar restitution orders, and Kilpatrick's historic resignation from office. 

Here is a full breakdown of the background, the cover-up, and the legal consequences served to the key figures.

---

### **The Background: The Lawsuit and the Cover-Up**

The roots of the scandal trace back to 2003, when Gary Brown, the head of the Detroit Police Department’s Internal Affairs unit, and Harold Nelthrope, a mayor’s security detail officer, were ousted from their positions. The officers filed a whistleblower lawsuit against Kilpatrick and the City of Detroit, claiming they were unlawfully terminated because they were investigating rumors of misdeeds by the mayor’s security detail—including allegations of an unbridled party at the mayor's official residence, the Manoogian Mansion.

During a August 2007 civil trial, the city defended itself by arguing that Brown was not fired, but rather that his position was eliminated due to budget cuts, and that Beatty and Kilpatrick had no romantic connection that would influence city decisions.

Under oath, both Kilpatrick and Beatty emphatically denied having an extra-marital affair or orchestrating the firing of Brown.
* "I think it's insulting, I think it's ridiculous," Kilpatrick testified when asked about a romantic involvement with Beatty.
* Beatty similarly denied the affair and testified that she made the independent decision to fire Brown based on performance issues.

Relying on their sworn testimony, the city lost the trial, and a jury awarded $6.5 million to the whistleblowing officers. Kilpatrick publicly vowed to appeal, claiming innocence. However, behind closed doors, the mayor quietly moved to settle the case—along with another related police lawsuit—for $8.4 million of taxpayer money, explicitly structuring the settlement agreement to keep trial exhibits confidential.

---

### **The Smoking Gun: The Text Messages**

The cover-up unraveled in January 2008, when reporters Jim Schaefer and M.L. Elrick of the *Detroit Free Press* obtained and published thousands of text messages sent between Kilpatrick and Beatty on their city-issued SkyTel pagers during 2002 and 2003.

The texts provided undeniable proof that both officials had committed perjury. The messages were filled with explicit romantic exchanges, but more critically, they directly linked their personal relationship to official city business and the firing of Gary Brown.

In one text sent shortly after Brown’s dismissal, Beatty wrote to Kilpatrick: 
> *"I'm worried about this Gary Brown thing. It's ridiculous how he is trying to turn this around on us."*

Kilpatrick replied: 
> *"It's not going to work. He's done."*

Other texts showed Beatty asking, *"All stress aside... have you thought about loving me today?"* to which Kilpatrick replied, *"I've thought about it all day."*

The revelation proved that Kilpatrick had used $8.4 million in taxpayer funds to settle the whistleblower lawsuit primarily to conceal the text messages and protect himself and Beatty from perjury charges.

---

### **The Charges and Legal Consequences**

In March 2008, Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy filed a multi-count felony indictment against both Kilpatrick and Beatty, stating, "Public office is a public trust... this case is about lying under oath."

Faced with overwhelming evidence, both defendants eventually struck plea deals to avoid lengthy prison sentences.

#### **1. Kwame Kilpatrick**
On September 4, 2008, after months of defying calls to resign, Mayor Kilpatrick pleaded guilty in Wayne County Circuit Court to two felony counts of **obstruction of justice**. He also entered a plea of no contest to assault in a separate incident involving a police officer who was trying to serve a subpoena to one of Kilpatrick's friends.

**The Legal Penalties:**
* **Resignation:** Forced to resign as Mayor of Detroit, effective September 18, 2008 (ending his six-year tenure).
* **Jail Time:** Sentenced to **120 days in the Wayne County Jail**. He served 99 days before being released for good behavior.
* **Restitution:** Ordered to pay **$1 million in restitution** to the City of Detroit.
* **Probation:** Sentenced to **5 years of probation**.
* **Loss of Law License:** Forced to surrender his license to practice law in the state of Michigan.
* **Public Office Ban:** Barred from running for public office for five years.

*Note: Kilpatrick’s legal troubles did not end here. In 2010, Judge David Groner found Kilpatrick in violation of his probation for hiding assets to avoid paying his $1 million restitution, resulting in a 1.5-to-5-year state prison sentence. Later, in 2013, Kilpatrick was convicted in a massive separate federal public-corruption case and sentenced to 28 years in federal prison (a sentence commuted by President Donald Trump in January 2021).*

#### **2. Christine Beatty**
In December 2008, former Chief of Staff Christine Beatty followed suit, pleading guilty to two felony counts of **misconduct in office**.

During her court appearance, a tearful Beatty took full responsibility, stating: "I lied under oath... I am deeply sorry for the pain and embarrassment I have brought to the citizens of Detroit."

**The Legal Penalties:**
* **Jail Time:** Sentenced by Judge David Groner to **120 days in the Wayne County Jail** (she served 69 days).
* **Probation:** Sentenced to **5 years of probation**.
* **Restitution:** Ordered to pay **$100,000 in restitution** to the City of Detroit.

---

### **The Legacy**

The text-message scandal reshaped the political landscape of Detroit. Beyond the immediate jail terms for Beatty and Kilpatrick, the scandal shattered public trust, crippled the city's finances by forcing millions in legal settlements, and set off a chain reaction of federal investigations. 

Ultimately, the text messages exposed not only a hidden affair, but a deliberate effort to abuse the power of the Mayor's office, misuse taxpayer money, and subvert the judicial system.

"I accept full responsibility for my actions," a tearful Beatty told the court prior to sentencing. "To the citizens of Detroit, I am deeply, deeply sorry for the pain and disappointment I have caused you."

### The Plea Deal: Charges Dropped and Reduced

Beatty’s jail sentence comes as part of a negotiated plea agreement reached with Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy. 

Under the terms of the deal, Beatty pleaded guilty to two felony counts of misconduct in office. In exchange, prosecutors dropped severe perjury charges—which carried a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison—as well as charges of obstruction of justice and conspiracy. 

Without the plea deal, Beatty faced seven felony counts that could have put her behind bars for more than a decade. The 120-day sentence mirrors the plea deal accepted late last year by her former boss and lover, Kwame Kilpatrick, who resigned as mayor in September after pleading guilty to similar misconduct charges.

"This was never about politics," Prosecutor Worthy said following the hearing. "This was about holding public officials accountable when they lie under oath and abuse the public trust."

### The Roots: The Gary Brown Whistleblower Lawsuit

The criminal charges against Beatty and Kilpatrick stemmed directly from lies told during a 2007 civil trial involving former Detroit Deputy Police Chief Gary Brown. 

The background of the case dates back to 2003, when Brown, a veteran officer heading the Detroit Police Department’s Internal Controls Division, began investigating alleged misconduct within the mayor’s inner circle. Among the matters Brown’s unit was examining were allegations of an unbridled mayoral security detail and rumors surrounding an alleged wild party at the mayor’s official residence, the Manoogian Mansion—an event that allegedly involved exotic dancers.

Before Brown could complete his investigations, Kilpatrick abruptly fired him. Brown, alongside fellow officer Harold Nelthrope, filed a whistleblower lawsuit against Kilpatrick, Beatty, and the city of Detroit, alleging they were terminated in retaliation for trying to expose official wrongdoing.

During the August 2007 civil trial, the case hinged on two critical questions: Did Kilpatrick and Beatty have an intimate relationship that influenced city decisions, and did they fire Gary Brown to cover up internal investigations?

On the witness stand, under oath, both Beatty and Kilpatrick vehemently denied having a romantic relationship. Furthermore, Beatty testified that she alone made the decision to fire Gary Brown due to performance issues, swearing that Kilpatrick was not involved in the firing and that it had nothing to do with Brown’s investigations.

Relying on their testimony, the defense fought the suit, but the jury ultimately sided with the officers, awarding Brown and Nelthrope $6.5 million. Rather than appeal, Kilpatrick quietly authorized a secret $9 million settlement using taxpayer funds—a move designed to keep key evidence from reaching the public.

### The Text Messages: Lies Unraveled

That secret evidence came to light in January 2008, when *The Detroit Free Press* obtained and published thousands of text messages sent to and from Beatty’s city-issued SkyTel pager during 2002 and 2003.

The text messages directly contradicted Beatty’s and Kilpatrick’s sworn court testimony, exposing both their romantic affair and their coordinated effort to oust Gary Brown.

In one intimate exchange from September 2003, Beatty asked Kilpatrick: *"I'm madly in love with you."* Kilpatrick responded: *"I hope you feel that way for a long time. I love you, too."*

More damaging to their legal standing were texts discussing Gary Brown. In May 2003, as Brown’s internal investigation escalated, Beatty texted Kilpatrick: *"They are trying to frame you on the whole Manoogian Mansion thing."* 

Later, Beatty texted: *"We won't even make it to the election. We're staying in the paper. We're sick. Gotta do something."*

Kilpatrick texted back: *"Gotta fire brown."* 

Beatty replied: *"I agree."*

The publication of the text messages shattered the defense presented in the civil trial, proving that both Beatty and the mayor had committed perjury while testifying. The revelations prompted Prosecutor Worthy to launch a criminal investigation, culminating in multi-count felony indictments against both officials in March 2008.

### Moving Forward

For Gary Brown, Beatty’s sentencing offers a sense of vindication after years of personal and professional turmoil. Brown, who maintained he was simply doing his job as a police officer, welcomed the resolution of the criminal cases.

"The truth finally came out," Brown said in a recent interview. "It was never about bringing down a mayor or his chief of staff; it was about integrity in public service."

Beatty is scheduled to report to the Wayne County Jail on January 5 to begin serving her 120-day term. Upon her release, she will begin her five-year probation period, during which she must make monthly payments toward her $100,000 restitution fine.

Kilpatrick, who completed his 120-day jail sentence earlier this month, remains on probation, though he still faces ongoing federal investigations regarding city contracts and municipal finances.

For Detroit, a city attempting to navigate severe economic hardship, the end of Beatty’s court saga marks a painful but necessary step toward closing one of the stormiest political eras in municipal history.
